text: A microwave oven uses an oscillating electric field to heat food. Metal conducts electricity, so the field drives strong currents along its surface. Those currents convert part of the microwave energy into heat, and the metal can reflect energy back toward its source. The violent sparks come from arcing: sharp edges and folds concentrate the field, and if two conductors are close, the air between them can break down into plasma. That is why crumpled foil or fork tines often spark, while smooth containers may be less risky. The reaction is a conductor response, not a chemical change.
